sections.history: Oppiliappan Koil, the Thiruvinnagar of the hymns, lies beside the town of Thirunageswaram, about seven kilometres from Kumbakonam. It is one of the 108 Divya Desams, the abodes of Vishnu sung by the Alvars in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, and among the most visited in Chola Nadu; three Alvars — Nammalvar, Peyalvar and Thirumangai Alvar — sang its lord. He is known by many names: Oppiliappan, 'the peerless one', Uppiliappan, Thiruvinnagarappan, Venkatachalapathy and Srinivasa, and the shrine has been called Vaikunta Nagaram, Markandeya Kshetram and Tulasi Vanam. Its origins are traced to the Medieval Chola period, when royal gifts to the temple are recorded, with further building under the Nayaks.
sections.architecture: The temple is built in the Dravidian style of the Kaveri delta, with a gopuram at its entrance and pillared halls leading to the sanctum, which is crowned by the Suddhananda Vimana. Within, the Lord stands with Bhudevi beside him, and the sage Markandeya, her foster-father, is part of the sanctum group. The temple tank is the Ahoratra Pushkarini, its name meaning 'of day and night'.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells that Bhudevi, the Earth Goddess, appeared here beneath a tulasi plant, where the sage Markandeya found her and raised her as his daughter. When she came of age the Lord arrived as an old man and asked for her hand. Markandeya demurred: she was so young, he said, that she did not even know how much salt to put in food. The Lord replied that he would gladly eat whatever she cooked, salt or none. To this day the offerings here are prepared without salt, and the Lord is Oppiliappan — the one without equal.
sections.festivals: Sravanam, the star held sacred to the Lord, is observed every month, and the celestial wedding of Oppiliappan and Bhudevi is celebrated on Sravanam in the month of Aippasi (October–November). Rama Navami and Vaikunta Ekadashi in Margazhi (December–January) draw large crowds from across the Kaveri delta. Check the temple's calendar for current dates.
sections.experience: Oppiliappan is a busy, beloved temple where devotees hold the Lord to be one with Srinivasa of Tirupati, whose name he shares. Taste the salt-free prasadam, a quiet lesson in the legend. The Saiva Naganathar temple of Thirunageswaram, one of the Navagraha shrines, stands in the same town, and Kumbakonam's many temples are minutes away.

visit.timings: Open daily for morning and evening darshan, with a midday closure; festival days are the busiest. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is removed before entering. Follow posted rules and the guidance of the priests.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow posted rules and the guidance of the priests.
visit.gettingThere: Oppiliappan Koil is beside Thirunageswaram, about 7 km from Kumbakonam in Thanjavur district, and is easily reached by town bus, auto-rickshaw or taxi. Kumbakonam has the nearest railway station; Tiruchirappalli has the nearest airport.
